results.title: The Case for 4-Bit Precision: k-bit Inference Scaling Laws: Paper Review | by Sulbha Jain | Medium
results.content: A recent study, “The Case for 4-bit Precision: k-bit Inference Scaling Laws,” investigates how reducing the precision of large language model (LLM) weights affects both memory use and accuracy — key concerns for deploying massive models efficiently. **What’s the best bit-precision for LLM inference if you want the best accuracy for a given memory budget?**. * **4-bit precision is optimal:** For fixed model memory (total model bits), using 4-bit quantization for parameters consistently yields the highest zero-shot accuracy across all tested model families and sizes. * **Inference speed boost:** Lowering bit-precision not only cuts memory requirements but also significantly reduces inference latency, especially for small batch sizes where memory bandwidth is the bottleneck. * For zero-shot inference, always use 4-bit quantization with small block sizes and floating-point data types for best accuracy and efficiency. * If you need to trade off between model size and bit-precision, keep the precision at 4 bits and adjust the number of parameters instead of increasing bit-width.

results.title: Parameters vs FLOPs: Scaling Laws for Optimal Sparsity for Mixture-of-Experts Language Models - Apple Machine Learning Research
results.content: Parameters vs FLOPs: Scaling Laws for Optimal Sparsity for Mixture-of-Experts Language Models. We explore this relationship in the context of sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoEs) , which allow scaling the number of parameters without proportionally increasing the FLOPs per example. We find that under different constraints (e.g., parameter size and total training compute), there is an optimal level of sparsity that improves both training efficiency and model performance. These results provide a better understanding of the impact of sparsity in scaling laws for MoEs and complement existing works in this area, offering insights for designing more efficient architectures. Sparse Mixtures of Experts (MoEs) are typically trained to operate at a fixed sparsity level, e.g. k in a top-k gating function. This global sparsity level determines an operating point on the accuracy/latency curve; currently, meeting multiple efficiency targets means training and maintaining multiple models. We propose a systematic method to determine the optimal data mixture for any target domain using scaling laws.

results.title: (PDF) Compression Scaling Laws:Unifying Sparsity and Quantization
results.content: We investigate how different compression techniques -- such as weight and activation quantization, and weight sparsity -- affect the scaling behavior of large language models (LLMs) during pretraining. Building on previous work showing that weight sparsity acts as a constant multiplier on model size in scaling laws, we demonstrate that this "effective parameter" scaling pattern extends to quantization as well. Specifically, we establish that weight-only quantization achieves strong parameter efficiency multipliers, while full quantization of both weights and activations shows diminishing returns at lower bitwidths. Our results suggest that different compression techniques can be unified under a common scaling law framework, enabling principled comparison and combination of these methods. results.title: Compression Scaling Laws: Unifying Sparsity and Quantization
results.content: Building on previous work showing that weight sparsity acts as a constant multiplier on model size in scaling laws, we demonstrate that this “effective parameter” scaling pattern extends to quantization as well. Model Compression, Large Language Models, Scaling Laws, Sparsity, Quantization. Notably, in the case of sparsity scaling laws, longer training durations were actually *necesary* to reach optimality for training over compressed models (Frantar et al., 2024). We then validate and analyze compression scaling laws for weight-only quantization, weight-and-activation quantization, and sparsity, in Section 2. While scaling behaviour of weight-sparsity is studied in depth in previous work (Frantar et al., 2024), we revisit it here under a different setup: for decoder-only architectures, larger models, and better tuned training parameters. For quantization-aware training, BitNet (Wang et al., 2023) and follow-up work (Ma et al., 2024; Kaushal et al., 2024) demonstrated stable training with binary and ternary weights, although a precise comparison against dense model scaling is not possible in their setting given the different hyper-parameters used.
